text.description: The University of Zurich, known as UZH, is the largest university in Switzerland, with around 28,700 students. It was founded in 1833 and was the first university in Europe set up by a state rather than by a monarch or the church. Its main building on Rämistrasse 71 dates from 1914 and was designed by the architect Karl Moser. The university is spread across the city. The main building has a tower and a long, palace-like facade. The view is from the Lindenhof hilltop, looking across the Limmat. From there the tower and facade rise above the Predigerkirche and the old town rooftops, so the university becomes the backdrop to a layered city scene. This is the usual postcard framing of the campus skyline. Take a wide shot first to get the whole scene, then a closer one to pick out the tower. If you have time, two other angles are worth a look. The Bahnhofbrücke gives a view up the slope across the river and rail approach, though check the angle on the map before relying on it. The forecourt at Rämistrasse 71 shows the facade up close, with its stairs, sculptures and lamp stands in the foreground. The forecourt is an entrance area, so check for any event or construction closures.
text.geographic_location: The University of Zurich main building is at Rämistrasse 71 in Zurich. The viewpoint is the Lindenhof hilltop, which looks across the Limmat towards the main building.
text.directions_text: From there, the university's main building is about 500 m to the south-east. The view from the Lindenhof looks north-east across the Limmat, so check the direction on the map before you set up. Then walk towards Rämistrasse 71. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole scene of rooftops, church and university. Then switch to telephoto (2x-3x, or up to 5x on some phones) to pick out the tower and facade. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of foreground and sky, as it makes the university look small and distant.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Lindenhof (hilltop, looking north-east across the Limmat towards the main building). The main building's tower and facade rising above the Predigerkirche and the old town rooftops, with the university as the backdrop. Check where the building sits on the map before you set up.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the tower on one of the vertical lines. Let the Predigerkirche and the rooftops fill the lower part of the frame so the university sits behind them. Keep the phone level so the building does not lean. For a different view, the Bahnhofbrücke and the Rämistrasse 71 forecourt are the two alternatives, as described above.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the facade keeps its detail. Hold the phone steady with both hands and take a few frames in a row.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Check the light on the day, as the view depends on the weather and the season.

name: Zürich Hauptbahnhof
label: Zurich Hauptbahnhof
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Bahnhofbrücke' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Bahnhofbrücke' (way/53275979): middle (63 m across); moved 35 m off water.

text.description:
Zürich Hauptbahnhof, or Zürich HB, is the largest railway station in Switzerland and one of the busiest in Europe. It sits at the northern end of Bahnhofstrasse, and its main entrance is a grand triumphal arch. The sandstone neo-Renaissance building opened in 1871 to a design by Jakob Friedrich Wanner. In front of the arch stands a monument to the railway pioneer Alfred Escher. The first station on this site opened in 1847 for the line to Baden, so the area has been a railway gateway for well over 150 years.

The best-known view is from the Bahnhofbrücke, the bridge over the Limmat directly opposite the station. From the upstream side you look back at the station front with the riverbank beside it. Trams often cross the bridge in the foreground, which adds movement and a clear sense of place. The arch and the long stone front are the main subject, so keep the lines straight and give the building room.

The bridge is busy, so take your time and stay clear of the tram lines and the pavement edge. If you want a quieter view, the green space of Platzspitz is another option, and the Negrellisteg may give an elevated view of the track field. Both are suggestions to try rather than certain views, so have a look when you arrive.
text.geographic_location: The station is in central Zurich, at the northern end of the Altstadt and of Bahnhofstrasse, close to where the Limmat and Sihl rivers meet. The Bahnhofbrücke crosses the Limmat just opposite the station front.
text.directions_text: The Bahnhofbrücke is near it, so head for the bridge and look back at the station. From the station front, walk towards the river and the bridge. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the station front, the riverbank and a passing tram into one picture. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view of the arch. If your phone has a telephoto (2x or more), use it for the details of the arch.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Bahnhofbrücke (upstream side, looking back toward the station). The station front and the Limmat riverbank framed together, with trams often crossing the bridge in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the building's vertical edges with them, so the arch does not lean. Keep the bridge and a little water in the lower part of the frame to add depth. For a different view, Platzspitz and the Negrellisteg are suggestions that may give a quieter or higher view, so have a look when you arrive.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stone facade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is washing out. Try a Live Photo when a tram is passing, so you can pick the best frame afterwards. Hold the phone steady with both hands and keep your elbows in.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people on the bridge. Weekday rush hours are busier. Check which way the light falls on the facade when you arrive.

text.access_note: The bridge and the area in front of the station are public spaces, but check the official site before you go for any works or restrictions, and before photographing inside the station.

name: Bahnhofstrasse
label: Bahnhofstrasse
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Bürkliplatz' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Bürkliplatz' (way/1469764193): middle (144 m across).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Bahnhofstrasse'.
notes: Famous shopping boulevard.

text.description: Bahnhofstrasse is Zurich's main downtown street, running about 1.4 km from the station square down to the lake. It is known as one of the world's most expensive shopping streets, but for a phone photographer the appeal is the long, straight line of facades, with trams gliding along it. The street only dates from 1864. That year the old city walls were pulled down and the ditch in front of them, once called the Fröschengraben (the 'Ditch of the Frogs'), was filled in. It was then renamed Bahnhofstrasse. Most of it is pedestrianised, though trams share it, and they add movement and a sense of scale to your photos. Toward the lake end is Paradeplatz, where two big Swiss banks have their headquarters and the well-known Confiserie Sprüngli chocolate shop and cafe stands. The best single picture is taken from Bürkliplatz at the lake end, looking back up the street towards the main station, with the tram lines and building fronts leading your eye into the city. If you want a different angle, Paradeplatz gives a busy tram crossing with bank buildings around it, and a central stretch of the street is quieter for shopfront views. In December the street is decorated with the Lucy light installation, so evening photos then look very different from the rest of the year.
text.geographic_location: Bahnhofstrasse is in the middle of Zurich's city centre. It links the main station (Zürich Hauptbahnhof) in the north with Bürkliplatz on the northern shore of Lake Zurich in the south, passing Paradeplatz on the way.
text.directions_text: Trams run along Bahnhofstrasse, so you can ride down from the main station area and get off at Bürkliplatz; check the VBZ tram map for the current lines. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the classic view up the street. Try the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the lake square and sky, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the distant facades and trams closer together.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Bürkliplatz (lake end of Bahnhofstrasse, at the tram stop and lakeside). A long, straight view back up Bahnhofstrasse toward the main station, with trams and the street's facades receding toward the city. Use the pavement or a tram island rather than the rails.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line up the tram tracks or the row of facades on one of the vertical lines, so the street runs straight into the picture. Wait for a tram to come into the frame, as it gives the shot life and scale. For a quieter alternative, walk up to Paradeplatz for the tram crossing and bank buildings, or pick a central stretch and shoot along the shopfronts.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the buildings in the middle distance to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky looks washed out. In the evening or the December lights, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a railing or your body. A Live Photo can catch a passing tram, so try one as well as a normal shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: There is no single fixed best time. Daytime gives clear views along the street, while in Advent and December the Lucy lights make the street worth visiting after dark. The street is busy during shopping hours, so earlier in the morning is likely to be calmer.

text.access_note: Bahnhofstrasse is an open public street, largely pedestrianised but with tram tracks, so stay on the pavement or a tram island.

text.description:
The Kunsthaus Zürich is Switzerland's biggest art museum by area, and its collection runs from the Middle Ages to contemporary art, with a focus on Swiss artists. The original building by Karl Moser and Robert Curjel opened in 1910. The large new wing by David Chipperfield, which began operating in October 2021, faces it across the street. The two are linked by a passage underneath.

The best photo here is taken from Heimplatz. Rodin's Gates of Hell stands in the foreground, the new wing rises behind it, and the building's facade picks up the movement of the square. That gives you a layered picture with art, architecture and everyday city life in one frame. Trams and pedestrians keep passing, so the scene changes from shot to shot, and a little patience pays off.

Take a wide shot first to show the sculpture in front of the building. Then move closer for a tighter picture of the sculpture alone, with the facade softly behind it. If you want a different angle, Rämistrasse gives a street-level view of the facade and extension, often with a tram going past. Stay on the pavement and keep clear of the tracks. Check for building works or temporary barriers on the square, as they can block the view.
text.geographic_location: In the city of Zurich, on Heimplatz, next to the Schauspielhaus Zürich and close to Rämistrasse.
text.directions_text: Take a tram to the stop Zürich, Kunsthaus, which is on Heimplatz between the museum and the Schauspielhaus Zürich. Check a tram map or timetable for the route from where you are staying. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the sculpture, the new wing and the square into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the sculpture or the facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Heimplatz (in front of the main entrance, facing the building's mirrored new extension). The museum's sloping, mirrored new wing with Rodin's Gates of Hell sculpture in the foreground and the square's street life around it. From here the new wing fills the background, Rodin's Gates of Hell sits in front of it, and the life of the square surrounds both.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the sculpture on one of the lower intersections, with the facade rising behind it. Wait for people or a tram to pass for a lively shot, or keep the frame empty for a calmer one. If you want something different, walk to Rämistrasse for a street-level view of the facade, ideally with a tram passing. Keep to the pavement.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so bright reflections and sky do not wash out the building. Portrait mode can help with a close shot of the sculpture, but check the edges look natural. Live Photos can catch a passing tram.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft, even daylight, such as a bright overcast day, usually suits a reflective facade best. Quieter times of day make it easier to get a clear view of the sculpture.

text.access_note: Heimplatz is a public square, but the museum itself is a ticketed attraction, so check the official site before you go for entry details and any temporary closures.

name: Grossmünster
label: Grossmünster
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Münsterbrücke' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Münsterbrücke' (way/368261937): middle (69 m across); moved 35 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/36916418: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Grossmünster' (75 m across).
notes: Twin-towered Romanesque church, symbol of Zurich.

text.description:
The Grossmünster is Zurich's great Romanesque church, and its twin towers are probably the most recognised sight in the city. Building began around 1100 and the church was inaugurated around 1220. The towers went up between 1487 and 1492. Their wooden steeples burnt down in 1763, and the neo-Gothic tops you see now were finished in 1787. It also matters in history: Huldrych Zwingli started the Swiss-German Reformation from here, from 1520.

It photographs well because the two towers stand tall above the Limmat, so the river, the bridge and the church all fit in one frame. The best-known view is from Münsterbrücke. Most photos taken on the bridge face the neighbouring Fraumünster, so turn around to frame the Grossmünster instead. Keep both towers fully in the frame and let the water fill the lower part of the picture.

If the bridge is crowded, Lindenhof gives a view over the Limmat and the Niederdorf rooftops to the twin towers. Wühre, across the water, is good at night with the tram lights and the river in the frame. Scaffolding and interior renovation have been reported on earlier visits, so check the current state before you go.
text.geographic_location: The Grossmünster stands beside the Limmat in Zurich, facing the Fraumünster across the water.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stops are listed for this spot, so head for the Limmat riverbank in Zurich. Münsterbrücke crosses the river right next to the church. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x), which shows the towers, the river and the bridge together. Try the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more water and sky, but keep the towers away from the edges of the frame, where they can stretch. A 2x or 3x telephoto lens gives a tighter shot of the towers if your phone has one.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Münsterbrücke (facing north toward the church from the bridge, with the Limmat on both sides of the frame). The two Romanesque towers rising above the river, with the Limmat and the bridge in the foreground. Turn around so you face the church, which lies to the east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the towers on one of the vertical lines. Keep the phone level so the towers do not lean. Let the Limmat fill the lower third of the picture. If the bridge is busy, try Lindenhof or Wühre instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the church to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not turn white. In the evening, night mode helps with the lit-up church, but hold the phone against the bridge railing or brace your elbows to keep it steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Blue hour, when the church is lit up, gives the strongest picture.

text.access_note: The bridge is a public place, but the church is a place of worship and may have limited access or renovation work, so check the official site before you go.

notes: Shaded hilltop square with a view over the old town and Limmat.

text.description:
The Lindenhof is a car-free hilltop square and park in the old town of Zurich, on the left bank of the Limmat beside the Schipfe. Its name means 'Tilia Courtyard'. The site has a long history: a Roman castle stood here, followed by a Carolingian royal residence. In 1747 a second-century Roman tombstone was found here, carrying the oldest known mention of Turicum, the Roman name for Zurich. In 1798 the citizens of Zurich swore their oath to the Helvetic Republic's constitution on this spot.

For photographers the appeal is the height. From the eastern edge, along the old wall and balustrade, you look across the Limmat to the Old Town waterfront, with the twin towers of the Grossmünster framed on the far bank. This is the classic postcard view of the city. The wall is often busy on sunny days, so arrive early or be ready to wait a minute for a gap.

Take one wide shot to show the whole river frontage, then a closer one of the towers and rooftops. Before you leave, turn round and look at the square itself, with its trees and the old buildings around it. It is a pleasant place to slow down and look before you shoot.
text.geographic_location: The Lindenhof is in Zurich's old town, on the left (west) side of the Limmat river, on a hill above the Schipfe. The view from its eastern edge looks across the river to the Old Town waterfront.
text.directions_text: Start from the old town of Zurich, on the left bank of the Limmat near the Schipfe, where the Lindenhof hill rises above the river. The Lindenhof is a car-free hilltop in the old town, so the last stretch is on foot and uphill. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole river frontage and sky. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the Old Town. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the Grossmünster's twin towers.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Lindenhof (eastern edge, the balustrade / old wall along the hilltop). Across the Limmat to the Old Town waterfront, with the Grossmünster's twin towers framed on the far bank.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the river's edge with a horizontal line so the waterfront sits level. Put the twin towers off-centre, on a third, with rooftops and water around them. If people are leaning on the wall, keep the wall low in the frame, or wait a moment for a clearer gap.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the towers to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky looks washed out. Hold the phone steady against the balustrade, or lean your elbows on it, for sharper zoomed shots.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and the Old Town facades look warmer. Early also means fewer people along the wall.

text.access_note: The Lindenhof is an open public park and square, and no closures or restrictions are known, but check the official site before you go.

name: Swiss National Museum
label: Swiss National Museum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Platzspitz' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Platzspitz' (way/88454956): middle (51 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/4281153: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Landesmuseum' (195 m across).
notes: Castle-like museum of Swiss cultural history.

text.description:
The Swiss National Museum looks like a fairy-tale chateau dropped beside Zurich's main railway station, and that is exactly why it photographs so well. Gustav Gull built it in 1898 in the historicist style, modelled on French Renaissance city chateaux, with dozens of towers, courtyards and a park on the peninsula between the rivers Sihl and Limmat. The museum was expanded between 2013 and 2016, but the old castle silhouette is still the part visitors want to capture.

The best frame is from Platzspitz park, looking across the water. From the park lawns and the Platzpromenade you can see the towers rising above the trees, with the river in the foreground. It is the usual place to fit in the whole castle outline, and the trees and water add layers to the picture. If you would like a quieter angle, Sihlquai gives a view across the Sihl towards the towers, with the park trees and the meeting of the Sihl and the Schanzengraben canal in the frame. Inside the museum grounds, the courtyard is the place for the towers and arched windows up close.

Take a few shots from different spots along the path rather than just one: even small steps left or right change how the towers line up behind the trees. Photography rules can differ inside the museum, particularly for temporary exhibitions, so check before you shoot indoors.
text.geographic_location: The museum is in Zurich's Old Town district, right next to Zürich Hauptbahnhof and the Platzspitz park, on the tongue of land between the rivers Sihl and Limmat.
text.directions_text: Start at Zürich HB, the main railway station, which sits right next to the museum; the closest tram/trolleybus stop is Bahnhofquai/HB. The museum building lies to the south-east of it, about 2 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to fit the whole castle and the trees in one frame. Switch to the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pick out the towers, and use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you move closer and want the full height of a tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Platzspitz (park lawns and Platzpromenade, facing the museum across the water). The neo-Gothic castle silhouette of the museum rising above the trees of the Platzspitz park, with the river in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the towers on the upper line, with the river along the bottom third. Let a few tree branches frame the edges, but keep the rooflines clear. For a different angle, Sihlquai gives a quieter view across the Sihl towards the towers. Panorama mode can help if you want the full width of the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the castle to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky stays pale blue or soft grey instead of turning white. Hold the phone steady with both hands, and take a couple of shots in case of ripples or passers-by.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the stonework and the water. Midday sun can be harsh, so use the exposure slider to keep the details.

text.access_note: Platzspitz is a public park, but entry to the museum itself may be ticketed and photo rules can differ for temporary exhibitions, so check the official site before you go.

name: Fraumünster
label: Fraumünster
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Münsterbrücke' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Münsterbrücke' (way/368261937): middle (69 m across); moved 35 m off water.

notes: Church known for its Chagall windows and slender spire.

text.description:
The Fraumünster is one of Zurich's four main churches, standing right beside the Limmat in central Zurich. It was built on the remains of an abbey for aristocratic women, founded in 853 by Louis the German for his daughter Hildegard. For centuries the abbess held great power in the city. The abbey was dissolved in 1524 during the Reformation, and today the church belongs to the Evangelical Reformed Church of the canton of Zurich. Inside, the choir has five large stained glass windows by Marc Chagall, installed in 1970, and the organ has 6,959 pipes, the most in the canton.

For a phone photo, the best exterior view is from Münsterbrücke. The church spire and the river sit together in one frame, so you get the water, the tower and the old buildings in a single shot. When you turn round, the Grossmünster is in view on the other side, which gives you a second picture from the same spot. If you have time, Lindenhofplatz gives a higher view over the Old Town and the river bend, and Münsterhof, the square in front of the church, is good for a close, ground-level shot of the clock face and facade. Photography of the Chagall windows inside is often restricted, so treat the exterior as your main subject and check the signs at the door.
text.geographic_location: The Fraumünster stands beside the Limmat in central Zurich, next to Münsterhof square.
text.directions_text: Head for the Limmat in central Zurich and ask for Münsterbrücke. Stand in the middle of the bridge and face west towards the church. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to fit the spire, the river and the bridge edge in one frame. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the spire and clock detail. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only from Münsterhof, where you are close to the facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Münsterbrücke (middle of the bridge, facing the church at the west end). The church spire and the Limmat river appear in one frame, with the Grossmünster visible when you turn around.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the spire up with a vertical line so the tower stands straight. Leave some of the river in the lower part of the frame so the water leads the eye to the church. Then turn around for a second shot of the Grossmünster. If you want a different view, Lindenhofplatz looks down over the Old Town with the church by the water, and Münsterhof gives a close angle on the clock face.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the spire to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour. At blue hour, switch on night mode and hold the phone still for the few seconds it needs.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Blue hour, when the sky still has colour and the lights are coming on along the river.

text.access_note: Check that the bridge is open and not blocked by construction before you go. The Fraumünster is a church with visitor rules and limits on photography inside, so check the official site and the signs at the door before you go.

name: Zurich Opera House
label: Opera House
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Sechseläutenplatz' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Sechseläutenplatz' (relation/15900079): middle (260 m across).

text.description:
The Zurich Opera House is the city's main opera and ballet theatre, and its ornate front is one of the easiest big buildings in Zurich to photograph. It faces a wide, open plaza, so you can stand back and get the whole facade in one frame. The front is white and grey stone, decorated with busts of Weber, Wagner and Mozart, and a few more figures including Schiller, Shakespeare and Goethe. The opera company has been based here since 1891. The original theatre was designed by the Viennese architects Fellner & Helmer, built in only 16 months after the earlier theatre burnt down, and was the first opera house in Europe with electric lighting. The building was rebuilt in the early 1980s, and the auditorium inside seats about 1100 people.

The best-known view is from across the square, facing the front of the building, with the lake close by. From there the facade sits neatly in the frame with open space around it, which suits a phone held upright or on its side. Late afternoon puts sunlight on the stonework, and in the evening the lit building makes a warm, moody picture. A second option is the Bellevue end of the plaza, where you see the opera with the lake and surrounding buildings behind it. Check the plaza for event stands or public screenings, as these can block the view.
text.geographic_location: The Zurich Opera House stands on Sechseläutenplatz, a pedestrian plaza in central Zurich close to the lake, with the Bellevue end of the plaza nearby.
text.directions_text: Head for Sechseläutenplatz, or for the Bellevue end of the plaza. Walk onto the open square and stop on the side facing the opera's front. From there the opera house lies to the south-east, about 1 minute on foot away, so you can take your photos before walking closer. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close, then try the default lens (1x) from further back for a more natural look. Use telephoto (2x-5x) for the busts and stone detail above the entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Sechseläutenplatz (across the square from the opera's front facade, facing the building). The full neo-Baroque white stone facade of the opera house, framed by the open pedestrian plaza, with the lake nearby.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the building up so its vertical edges stay straight; keep the phone level and avoid tilting it upwards. Leave some open plaza in the foreground to give the building room. For a different view, walk to the Bellevue end of the plaza and photograph the opera with the lake and surrounding buildings behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the pale stone keeps its detail. In the evening, use night mode and hold the phone steady against your body or a railing; the lit building will be sharper if you stay still for the full exposure.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon for sunlight on the facade, or evening when the building is lit.

text.access_note: The facade can be photographed from the open public plaza; if you want to go inside or take photos indoors, check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Holding the phone level and keeping the verticals straight helps avoid the building looking tilted.

name: Bürkliplatz, Zurich
label: Bürkliplatz
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Bürkliterrasse' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Bürkliterrasse' (relation/9285957): middle (67 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1469764193: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Bürkliplatz' (144 m across).
notes: Lake promenade and boat landing at the Limmat outflow.

text.description:
Bürkliplatz is the busy square where Zurich's Bahnhofstrasse meets the lake. Trams, lake boats and the lakeside promenades all come together here. It is named after Arnold Bürkli, and the promenades and terrace were built in the 1880s. The Bürkliterrasse on the lake side was inaugurated in 1887. It was originally topped with two large plaster lions, which the townspeople disliked, and they were taken down two years later. Today a sculpture by Hermann Hubacher, from 1952, shows Zeus as an eagle carrying off Ganymede. The shaded square behind it, the Stadthausanlage, has a market on Fridays and a flea market on Saturdays, so expect more people then.

It photographs well because the view is open. From the railing on the terrace you look straight down the length of Lake Zurich, with water in the foreground and the line of the Alps far behind it. Nothing blocks the view, and the sky takes up much of the frame, so the picture changes a lot with the weather. A clear morning after rain gives the sharpest mountains. For variety, turn round for the trees, the fountain and the old music pavilion on the square. Boats at the landing stage make a lively foreground, and the Quaibrücke next door gives a different angle.
text.geographic_location: Bürkliplatz is in central Zurich, on the lake at the lower end of Bahnhofstrasse. It sits just west of the Quaibrücke, where the Limmat leaves the lake.
text.directions_text: From the Bahnhofstrasse area or the Old Town, walk towards the lake and the square is at the water's edge, just west of the Quaibrücke. The square has a tram stop of the same name, served by lines 2, 5, 8, 9 and 11. Once on the square, head to the southern edge, where the terrace railing faces the lake. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the classic lake view. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to include more water and sky. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pull the distant mountain edge closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Bürkliterrasse (southern edge of the square, at the railing). The lake running south toward the Alps, with the water in the foreground and the distant mountain edge behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Rest your phone near the railing and keep the horizon level using the gridlines. Put the water in the lower third and let the mountains and sky fill the rest. If the railing intrudes, hold the phone just above it. For a different view, walk onto the Quaibrücke: from there you can frame the Old Town skyline, with the Grossmünster's twin towers and the Peterskirche clock tower, or turn the other way to the lake. The Schifflände landing stage is another option, with boats in the foreground and the hills behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the mountains to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour and detail. If the Alps look faint, try the telephoto lens and keep the shot simple.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when the sky is pale and the water picks up the first colours. A clear morning after rain, or one in autumn or winter, can give the clearest mountain view.

text.access_note: The square and terrace are open public space, but the market and boat boarding can make it crowded; check the official site before you go for any events.
claims_not_in_sources: The Alps are not always visible from the terrace; the view depends on the weather and haze.
The square and terrace are free to enter and are not a ticketed site.
The terrace railing may get in the way of some phone shots, so holding the phone slightly above it can help.

name: Paradeplatz
label: Paradeplatz
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Bahnhofstrasse' (1 web pages); placed at the stretch of Bahnhofstrasse nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/905841: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Paradeplatz' (123 m across).
notes: Central square with trams and Confiserie Sprüngli.

text.description:
Paradeplatz is the square in the middle of downtown Zurich where Bahnhofstrasse meets the tram lines. It is closely tied to Swiss banking, with big bank buildings on its sides, and the older buildings make a good backdrop. The UBS building on the west side dates from 1897–1899, the Sprüngli confectioner on the south side opened in 1859, and the hotel at the eastern end opened in 1838. Before that, the site was brought inside the town's walls in 1642 and was a livestock market in the 17th century. It took its present name in 1865, after Bahnhofstrasse was built.

For a phone photo, the most pleasing frame is not the square head-on but the stretch of Bahnhofstrasse running towards Bürkliplatz and the lake. The plane trees on both sides narrow the view and lead the eye down the street to the water, which suits daytime shots. If you want the whole square, step back and take a wide frame with the tram lines, the bank facades and the trams passing through. The square is closed to cars, but it is a busy tram hub, so keep well clear of the tracks and watch for traffic while you line up a picture. Allow a few minutes for a tram to pass through the frame, as it adds life to the shot.
text.geographic_location: Paradeplatz is in downtown Zurich, on Bahnhofstrasse, with Bürkliplatz further along towards the lake.
text.directions_text: Start from the centre of downtown Zurich and head for Bahnhofstrasse. The square is closed to cars but is a busy tram hub, so you can arrive by tram (Paradeplatz stop) or on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the tree-lined street view. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole square with trams and facades. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a tram or a facade detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Bahnhofstrasse (the stretch between Paradeplatz and Bürkliplatz, looking toward the lake). A tree-lined perspective down the street, with the plane trees framing the view toward the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the street in the centre so the rows of trees lead the eye to the lake. Keep the trees evenly placed on both sides and hold the phone level so the buildings don't lean. For a different view, turn back towards Paradeplatz and use the ultra-wide (0.5x) lens to catch the tram lines, the bank facades and a passing tram.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the far end of the street to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little if the sky looks washed out. Try a Live Photo to catch a tram gliding through, and stand clear of the tracks.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime suits the tree-lined view. Around dusk the city lights make it more atmospheric, but expect more people.

text.access_note: Paradeplatz is an open public square closed to cars, but it is a busy tram hub, so stay off the tracks.
claims_not_in_sources: Photography inside the bank buildings is generally not permitted.
Evening and blue-hour light with city lights is attractive but busier.
Plane trees line both sides of this stretch of Bahnhofstrasse.

name: Quaibrücke, Zurich
label: Quaibrücke
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Utoquai' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Utoquai nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/356474416: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Quaibrücke' (138 m across).

text.description: The Quaibrücke is the broad bridge where Lake Zurich narrows into the Limmat. It links Bürkliplatz on the western shore with Bellevueplatz on the eastern shore, and it carries road traffic, trams, cyclists and pedestrians. It dates from the 1880s. The bridge you see today replaced the original in 1984, when the old structure was slid aside on steel beams over a single weekend, and it was given extra width for pedestrians and bikes in 2015. It photographs well because of the setting. From the lakeside you see the long, low line of the bridge with trams crossing, and the church towers of the Fraumünster and St. Peter rising behind it, with the Bauschänzli nearby. It is a calmer place to stand than the bridge itself, which is busy with traffic and shakes slightly when a tram passes. Wait for a tram to cross if you want a little movement and colour in the frame. Keep the bridge's long line level with the gridlines, and leave room above it so the towers are not cut off. If you walk onto the bridge, you can turn the other way for the Limmat heading away from the lake, with the Fraumünster, St. Peter and Grossmünster towers on the skyline.
text.geographic_location: The Quaibrücke is in the centre of Zurich, where Lake Zurich flows into the Limmat. It links Bürkliplatz and Bellevueplatz, and the Utoquai runs along the eastern shore beside it.
text.directions_text: Take a tram to the Bellevue stop, at the eastern end of the bridge, or to Bürkliplatz on the western side. From Stadelhofen station it is about a 5-minute walk to the bridge. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the bridge with the towers behind it. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the Fraumünster and St. Peter closer. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of promenade and water in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Utoquai (lakeside promenade on the west bank, looking back at the bridge). The Quaibrücke seen from the lakeshore, with the Bauschänzli and the church towers of Fraumünster and St. Peter in the background. From here the photo shows the Quaibrücke with the Bauschänzli, the Fraumünster tower and St.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and put the bridge deck on a lower line so it stays level. Leave sky for the church towers. Wait for a tram to cross for a little life in the picture. If you walk onto the bridge as an alternative, face away from the lake to catch the Limmat and the three towers on the skyline.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the bridge to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky looks washed out. At dusk, use night mode and brace your elbows on the railing or a wall, because the promenade is busy and hand shake shows in long exposures. If you shoot from the bridge itself, wait for a gap between trams, as they make it vibrate.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day, the light should fall on the bridge face from behind you, and the promenade is likely to be quieter. Around dusk, with the lights coming on, night mode works well. Midday is the busiest and the flattest in light.

text.access_note: The bridge and the Utoquai are open public road and promenade, shared with trams, cyclists and walkers; check the official site before you go if works are planned.
claims_not_in_sources: Looking west from the Utoquai, morning light should fall on the face of the bridge from behind the photographer.
The promenade is likely to be quieter early in the day and busiest around midday.
In the evening, the bridge and towers are likely to look good with the lights on, suiting night mode.
Leaning on a railing or wall helps keep a phone steady in night mode.

name: Münsterbrücke, Zurich
label: Münsterbrücke
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Wühre' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Wühre nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/368261937: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Münsterbrücke' (69 m across).
notes: Bridge between Grossmünster and Fraumünster.

text.description: The Münsterbrücke is a broad stone bridge across the Limmat in the middle of Zurich's old town. It links the Grossmünster on the east bank with the Fraumünster on the west, and most people photograph it as a frame for those two churches. This cobbled riverside street runs along the west bank, close to the bridge. From there you can look across the water at the bridge area and the Grossmünster, with old framed houses beside you and the river in front. Guides suggest it as a quieter alternative to standing on the bridge itself. The bridge was opened in August 1838 and replaced an older wooden crossing. It has four flat arches and a smaller fifth arch over a former channel, black Jura marble on the pillars and cast-iron railings, and it is listed as a cultural property of national importance. Those details make good close-ups if you stand on the bridge's footpaths. Take a wide shot from Wühre first, with the river, the houses and the church towers in one frame. Then walk the short distance to the bridge for a second angle, such as the railings leading the eye towards the towers. Road traffic on the bridge is limited, and trams run along nearby Limmatquai rather than across the bridge, but stay on the footpaths and keep your phone steady near the kerb. The Wühre viewpoint comes from fewer guides than the bridge, so check it against what you see on the day.
text.geographic_location: The bridge is in the historic core of old Zurich, crossing the Limmat between Münsterhof on the west bank and Limmatquai on the east. It lies between the Quaibrücke and the Rathausbrücke, with the Fraumünster and Grossmünster at either end.
text.directions_text: Head for Limmatquai on the east bank, where tram lines 2, 4 and 15 run past, and cross the Münsterbrücke to the west bank. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the street, river and bridge together, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the Grossmünster's towers.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Wühre (west (left) bank of the Limmat, close to the bridge). A cobbled riverside street with old framed houses and the Grossmünster in view, which gives a view of the bridge area from the river's west bank. From here the Münsterbrücke area is to the east, across the water, with the Grossmünster in view and the cobbles and old framed houses beside you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the river or the bridge's lower edge on a bottom line, with the church towers rising above it. Let the old houses form one side of the frame. For a different view, walk onto the bridge footpath and shoot the Grossmünster's twin towers above the Limmat, or try the Rudolf-Brun-Brücke for a skyline looking north along the river.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the church towers to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the stonework keeps its detail. Hold the phone with both hands and keep to the footpaths, as the road can get busy.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is likely to be quieter on the street and the bridge. Soft light in the morning or evening usually suits the stone and the water.

text.access_note: The bridge area is part of the old town's pedestrian zone, but the bridge still has limited road traffic, so take care. Trams run on nearby Limmatquai, not across the bridge.

name: Sechseläutenplatz
label: Sechseläutenplatz
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Utoquai' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Utoquai nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/15900079: 'Die Schreitende', the best-known feature inside 'Sechseläutenplatz' (261 m across).
notes: Large square by the opera house.

text.description:
Sechseläutenplatz is the largest town square in Zurich, on the east shore of the lake just south of where the water flows out into the Limmat. Its name comes from Sechseläuten, the city's spring festival, which is held here in April. The surface is laid with about 110,000 long blocks of Vals quartzite, and the square covers roughly 16,000 square metres. It was redesigned and reopened in early 2014. Digging nearby in 2009 turned up remains of prehistoric pile dwellings.

It photographs well because it is so open: pale stone, young trees, the Opernhaus on one side and the lake promenade on the other. The best view is from Utoquai, the lakeside stretch opposite the square. Looking east from there you can frame the square, with the colourful flower boxes along the promenade as a foreground. The towers of the old town are also part of the view along this stretch of Utoquai, but they lie in a different direction from the square, so you may need to turn around to photograph them as a separate shot. Because the square is wide and flat, a simple, uncluttered shot often works best, so keep the horizon level and let the empty space do the work.

If you want a second angle, try Quaibrücke, which shows the square with the Opernhaus behind it, or Bellevueplatz at the northern edge, where the square meets the fountain and the opera house. The square hosts events on many days of the year (Circus Knie, Sechseläuten, a Christmas market), and stalls can block the view, so check the event calendar before you set out.
text.geographic_location: Sechseläutenplatz is in central Zurich on the east shore of Lake Zurich, just south of the lake outflow to the Limmat. It sits between the Opernhaus to the south and Bellevueplatz to the north, with the Utoquai promenade along its lake side.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stop is listed for this spot, so start from the Bellevue area at the northern edge of the square, or go by taxi or hired scooter and ask for Utoquai at the height of Sechseläutenplatz. From there the square's best-known feature, Die Schreitende, is about 1 minute on foot to the east. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the square as a whole. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the flower boxes large in the foreground. Use telephoto (2x or more) to pick out details of the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Utoquai (lakeside stretch opposite the square, at the height of Sechseläutenplatz). The square and the towers of the Zurich old town seen across the lake promenade, with flower boxes as a foreground. Face east towards the square, with the flower boxes along the bottom of the frame. The old-town towers are a separate view in another direction, so you may need to turn around for them.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the flower boxes along the lower third, with the square above them. Keep the phone level so the open square does not look tilted. If you have time, try a second shot from Quaibrücke, with the Opernhaus behind the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the middle of the square to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the pale stone and the sky both keep their detail. Take a few frames in case people walk through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually means fewer people and softer light. Whatever the time, check the event calendar first, since stalls and tents can fill the square.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space, but event set-ups can close or block parts of it, so check the official site before you go.

name: Polybahn
label: Polybahn
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Polyterrasse' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Polyterrasse' (way/192151233): middle (106 m across); moved 25 m off buildings.

text.description:
The Polybahn is a short red funicular that links Central with the Polyterrasse beside the main building of ETH Zurich. The railway takes its name from the old Polytechnikum, as the university was once called. It opened in 1889 and was first driven by water: a tank under the carriage was filled at the top and emptied at the bottom. It switched to electric drive in 1897 and was completely rebuilt in 1996. It was closed for refurbishment in spring 2021 and reopened on 17 September 2021. It is owned by UBS and run for them by Zurich's municipal transport operator. That mix of old tradition and modern upkeep is part of its charm.

For a phone photographer, the best picture is from the top, on the Polyterrasse, where you look out over Old Town rooftops and church towers, the Limmat, Lake Zurich and, on clear days, the Alps. Guides call it the classic Zurich skyline view. The funicular and its lower station make a second picture from near Central; one blog mentions a bridge-like track, so check the view on the ground.

Keep your phone ready for quick shots, as the cabins come and go and people cross the terrace. Trees block parts of the view, and summer haze can flatten the mountains, so take a few frames and pick the clearest.
text.geographic_location: The Polybahn runs up the slope between Central, near the Limmat, and the Polyterrasse by ETH Zurich's main building. The top station is also close to the Natural History Museum.
text.directions_text: Head for Central square and find the lower station of the Polybahn. The ride up takes about 100 seconds. Check the official site before you go for running times and tickets. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full skyline, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view of the rooftops. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the Grossmünster towers or a patch of the Alps.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Polyterrasse (west end of the balustrade, or the left-hand corner of the terrace). Old Town rooftops and church towers in the foreground, the Limmat and Lake Zurich in the middle distance, and the Alps on clear days. The funicular's line lies to the north-west of this point.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: The western balustrade gives a centred view of the Grossmünster towers. From the left-hand corner you can take a wide shot with no railing in the frame. Turn on gridlines to keep the horizon level, and let the rooftops fill the lower third. For the funicular itself, go down near Central and shoot the red cars and track, with the Limmat and lower station behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the distant towers to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour. If haze flattens the Alps, try a telephoto frame of the nearer rooftops instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset and golden hour, because the terrace faces west.

text.access_note: The Polyterrasse is an open public terrace; for riding the funicular, check the official site before you go.

name: St. Peter, Zurich
label: St. Peter Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Lindenhof' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Lindenhof' (relation/1693094): edge nearest the subject (1255 m across); moved 15 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/24701951: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'St. Peter' (54 m across).
notes: Church with the largest clock face in Europe.

text.description:
St. Peter is one of the four main churches of Zurich's old town, and its tower is the part most visitors photograph. The clock faces are huge: each is about 8.7 metres across, among the largest church clock faces in Europe. The tower is 64 metres tall and has a pointed wooden roof, re-covered in 1996 with larch shingles. The roof is the only wooden one in the city. The church stands beside the Lindenhof hill on a site with a very long history. An early church is recorded here from the 8th or 9th century, and the present building was consecrated in 1706.

It photographs well because the tower is tall, simple and easy to recognise. Face west from there to get the tower and clock face above the old town. The Lindenhof viewpoint is a separate spot, and it gives the classic Old Town view with the tower, the river and the Grossmünster towers. For a very different picture, walk down to St. Peterhofstatt, the square beside the church. There you can tilt the phone upwards and catch the giant clock face looming over the trees and old buildings. The Limmatquai, across the river, gives a third view, with the tower rising over the water and the guild houses.

Work on the church may mean some scaffolding on the tower or exterior, so check before you go. If you go inside, avoid flash during services.
text.geographic_location: St. Peter stands in the old town of Zurich, near the Limmat, right beside the Lindenhof hill and the square called St. Peterhofstatt.
text.directions_text: Head for the old town of Zurich and the Lindenhof hill. From there the church is a short stroll away, about 1 minute on foot, to the west. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the whole scene with the Limmat and the Grossmünster towers at the Lindenhof viewpoint. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x) to pick out the tower and the clock face. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only down in St. Peterhofstatt, for looking up at the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Lindenhof (eastern balustrade edge, looking back across the Limmat). St. Peter's tower and clock face seen from the hilltop above the old town, with the Limmat and the Grossmünster towers in the same frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the tower upright along one of the vertical lines. At the Lindenhof viewpoint, leave some river and rooftops at the bottom, and the Grossmünster towers to one side. For a different shot, try Limmatquai, where the tower rises over the water. Alternatively, in St. Peterhofstatt, hold the phone low and shoot upwards to fill the frame with the clock face and the trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower or the clock face to focus. Then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not turn white and the clock keeps its detail. Hold the phone steady against the balustrade or another solid support when you use telephoto.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or sunset, when the light is softer and the square is quieter.

text.access_note: Lindenhof and the square around the church are open public spaces, but the church and tower may be closed or under renovation, so check the official site before you go.

name: Zurich Town Hall
label: Rathaus
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Rathausbrücke' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Rathausbrücke' (way/8147286): middle (77 m across); moved 20 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/30067765: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Rathaus' (44 m across).
notes: Baroque guild-era town hall on the Limmat.

text.description: Zurich's Town Hall, the Rathaus, stands right on the Limmat, and that is what makes it work so well on a phone. Its walls rise straight from the water, so you get the building, the river and the old-town bank in one frame. It was built between 1694 and 1698 and replaced an earlier town hall from 1397. It served as the seat of government of the Republic of Zurich until 1798. The canton of Zurich has owned it since 1803, and today it houses both the cantonal parliament and the City Parliament. From here the riverside facade is framed across the Limmat with the water running along its walls, and guides point to this bridge for an unobstructed view. If you want a change, Münsterbrücke shows the Town Hall down the river with the water between you and the building. Wühre gives a closer, angled view with the guild houses in the foreground. Only the outside can be photographed, as the interior is not open to visitors. A renovation is planned, so scaffolding or covers may appear on the facade. Have a look when you arrive and, if the main view is covered, try one of the other two spots.
text.geographic_location: In Zurich's Altstadt, in the Rathaus quarter on the right bank of the Limmat, beside the Limmatquai and the Rathausbrücke, between Bellevue and Central.
text.directions_text: Head for the Rathaus quarter of the Altstadt on the east bank of the Limmat, along the Limmatquai between Bellevue and Central; the area is in the pedestrian old town. From there the Town Hall is about 23 m to the south-east, right beside the bridge. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole facade and the river. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the walls and windows. The ultra-wide (0.5x) only helps if you step in close, and it can make the building lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Rathausbrücke. The Town Hall's riverside facade framed across the Limmat, with the water flowing along its walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the building's vertical lines straight. Put the water in the lower third so the Town Hall seems to rise out of the river. If you want a second angle, Münsterbrücke gives a view down the Limmat with the river between you and the building. Wühre gives a closer view with the guild houses in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky or the water is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. Hold the phone steady with both hands, as people walk across the bridge.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or evening light, or an even overcast day, usually suits the facade and the water. Early in the day the bridge is likely to be quieter.

text.access_note: You can photograph the exterior from public bridges and streets; the interior is not open to visitors, so check the official site before you go, especially as renovation work may be under way.

name: Wasserkirche
label: Wasserkirche
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Münsterhof' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Münsterhof' (relation/8143995): middle (122 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/112795856: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Wasserkirche' (39 m across).
notes: Church standing in the Limmat next to Grossmünster.

text.description:
The Wasserkirche ("water church") sits on a small island in the river Limmat, between the Grossmünster and the Fraumünster, and is joined to the Helmhaus beside it. It is a good subject because the church, the Helmhaus, the river and the Grossmünster towers all fit into one view. The church is first mentioned around 1250. It was completely rebuilt, finishing in 1486. After the Reformation it became Zurich's first public library in 1634. The island was joined to the right bank in 1839 when the Limmatquai was built. The building is now used for services again and is listed as a Class A object of national importance. The Helmhaus has a stone hall dating from 1791.

The view suggested here is from Münsterhof, on the Stadthausquai side, looking across the Limmat. From there you see the Wasserkirche with the Helmhaus to its left and the Grossmünster in the background over the water. It is a quieter spot than the bridge. If you want a different angle, the Quaibrücke shows the church and the Grossmünster along the Limmatquai, and Lindenhof gives a raised view over the Old Town rooftops. Take a few frames with different amounts of river in the foreground. Keep the phone level so the church and the Helmhaus walls stay upright.
text.geographic_location: In the middle of Zurich's Old Town, on an island in the river Limmat between the Grossmünster and the Fraumünster, next to the Münsterbrücke and the Limmatquai.
text.directions_text: Head for Münsterhof in the Old Town, on the left bank of the Limmat, and stand on the Stadthausquai side facing the river. From there the Wasserkirche is to the east, about 3 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the church, the Helmhaus and the Grossmünster behind. Switch to 2x or more (telephoto, depending on your phone) for a tighter frame of the church and towers. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of river and sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Münsterhof (Stadthausquai side, looking across the Limmat). Wasserkirche with the Helmhaus to its left and the Grossmünster in the background, seen over the river.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the river along the lower third, with the church just off-centre. Keep the Helmhaus on the left and the Grossmünster towers above the roofline behind. For a second angle, the Quaibrücke is a good alternative, showing the church with the Grossmünster along the Limmatquai.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the church to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. Take a Live Photo if boats or passers-by are moving on the river, and pick the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Afternoon and early evening are likely to be kind, as the sun is then behind you and lights the church front. Early morning can be pleasant and quiet, but the sun will be behind the church, so expect a brighter sky.

text.access_note: The viewpoint is an open public square; for the inside of the church or the Helmhaus, check the official site before you go, as exhibitions and services may restrict photos.

name: Schipfe
label: Schipfe
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Limmatquai' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Limmatquai nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/3666748026: the OpenStreetMap point 'Schipfe'.
notes: Historic lane along the Limmat, the oldest part of the old town.

text.description:
The Schipfe is a small riverside quarter on the western bank of the Limmat, tucked below the Lindenhof hill in Zurich's old town. Its row of narrow, characterful houses runs right along the water, and from across the river they make a tidy, colourful band that suits a phone screen well. The name goes back to 1292, when it was written "Schüpfi", meaning a place where boats land. Historians also suggest the area was part of the civilian harbour of Roman Turicum, so the waterfront has been in use for a very long time. Today it is mostly homes, with a few small shops that are easy to miss.

The best overall picture is taken from the opposite bank, on Limmatquai, facing west. From there you see the old riverside houses with the Rathausbrücke at the left edge of the frame, and the water gives you a natural foreground. If you want a different angle, the Lindenhof above gives a high view down over the Schipfe rooftops and the river. You can also walk along the Schipfe itself for close views of the houses and the water. Keep the phone level so the rooflines do not lean, and wait for a gap in the passers-by on the pavement before you shoot.
text.geographic_location: The Schipfe is in Zurich's old town on the west bank of the Limmat, below the Lindenhof hill and just downstream of the Rathausbrücke, facing the Limmatquai on the opposite bank.
text.directions_text: Make for Limmatquai on the east bank of the Limmat, near the Rathausbrücke end, in Zurich's old town. Walking there means crossing a bridge such as the Rathausbrücke, which takes a few minutes. Once you have your shots from the east bank, you can walk along the Schipfe itself. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to frame the whole row of houses across the river. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want more water and sky, and check that the edges of the houses do not stretch. The telephoto (2x-3x, depending on your phone) is good for picking out a few facades or windows.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Limmatquai (east bank, facing west across the Limmat, near the Rathausbrücke end). The row of old riverside houses on the Schipfe bank, with the Rathausbrücke at the left edge of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the houses across the middle of the frame and let a strip of river fill the bottom. Keep the Rathausbrücke at the left edge as a frame. Turn on gridlines and line a horizontal grid line up with the water's edge so the scene stays straight. For a different view, walk up to the Lindenhof for a high shot down over the rooftops.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the houses to set focus and exposure. If the sky is bright, drag the exposure slider down a little so the facades keep their colour. A Live Photo can add a little movement from the water and passers-by.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning is likely to suit the houses best, because the sun is then behind you and lights the fronts. An evenly overcast day also works well. Late in the day, you will be shooting towards the light, so check the exposure.

text.access_note: The Schipfe is a public street along the Limmat and is free to photograph, but check on site for any closures or building work along the riverfront.

name: ETH Zurich
label: ETH Zurich
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Polyterrasse' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Polyterrasse' (way/192151233): middle (106 m across); moved 25 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/9379177: large area 'ETH Zürich, Zentrum' (944 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Terrace outside the main building with a city view.

text.description:
ETH Zurich is the Swiss federal technical university, and its main building is the best-known part of the Zentrum campus. It was built between 1858 and 1864 to designs by Gottfried Semper, in a neoclassical style with a heavy, rusticated ground level and tall columns above. The cupola was added when the building was enlarged in the early 1900s. Locally people still call the university 'Poly', after its original name as a federal polytechnic school. It was founded in 1854, and Albert Einstein is among its best-known associates.

It photographs well because the long facade faces a wide, open terrace, so you can step back and fit a lot in. Turn away from the building and the terrace also offers a separate view out towards the old town roofs, the Uetliberg hill beyond them and, on clear days, the Alps. Guides call this the classic view of the building.

For a clean wide shot of the facade, go to the left-hand corner of the terrace, where the railing stays out of the frame. Turn on your gridlines and keep the phone level so the facade does not lean. Wait for a gap in the people crossing the terrace, then take a few frames. If you have time, Lindenhof across the old town gives a more distant view of the campus on its hill. That is a different picture, not a close-up of the facade.
text.geographic_location: ETH Zurich's main building stands on the hillside above Zurich's old town, directly across the street from the University Hospital and next to the University of Zurich's main building. The Polyterrasse is the open terrace in front of it.
text.directions_text: Start at Central and take the Polybahn funicular up to the Polyterrasse; a fare applies, though the Zurich Card covers it. The terrace can also be reached on foot. Once you are on the terrace, the main building is directly in front of you. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole facade, and the terrace in front of it, into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the cupola or the roofline.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Polyterrasse (left-hand corner of the terrace, for a wide shot without the railing). The main building's facade across the terrace, with the old town, the Uetliberg hill in the distance, and on clear days the Alps. Face east and the main building lies ahead of you, across the terrace. Do not try to fit them into the same frame as the facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the facade up with the horizontal lines. Keep the phone level and at chest height, not tilted up, so the vertical lines stay straight. Leave some terrace in the foreground for depth. If you want a different view, Lindenhof gives a wider shot of the campus across the old town.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. For a wider sweep of the city when you look west, try panorama mode, and hold still while it records.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset, according to several guides, because the terrace faces west. On a clear evening the low light may suit both the facade and the distant view.

text.access_note: The terrace and the public areas of the main building are reported to be open to visitors without booking, but hours vary, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: At sunset the low western light should fall on the facade from behind someone standing on the terrace.
Keeping the phone level and using gridlines helps stop the facade leaning in the photo.
The telephoto lens can pick out details such as the cupola from the terrace.
Pedestrians crossing the terrace may spoil the frame, so waiting for gaps helps.
